A company deploys generative AI applications and wants to screen prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data leakage, and harmful content. Which Google Cloud offering fits?

A company's teams have launched many AI models and agents. Security leaders want to discover the AI assets in use, assess their risks, and protect them against threats across the AI lifecycle. Which offering fits?
AI Protection helps organizations inventory AI assets, assess and manage AI risks, and detect threats to AI workloads.

5.2 Describe the business value of Google's multilayered approach to cloud security
A CISO asks why Google Cloud's infrastructure is considered secure by design. Which answer is most accurate?
Google uses only off-the-shelf hardware with no custom security.
Google builds security into every layer, including proprietary data centers, purpose-built servers and networking, and custom security hardware and software.
Google doesn't encrypt data by default.
Google relies only on customers to secure its data centers.
Google designs its own data centers, servers, network, and security chips, building security into each layer, and encrypts data at rest by default.

A company wants employees to access internal web applications securely from anywhere without a VPN, with access granted based on user identity and context. Which Google Cloud product fits?
IAP controls access to applications based on identity and context, supporting a zero-trust approach without a VPN. The other products don't control application access.
5. Trust and Security with Google Cloud

A company stores customer support transcripts and must find and mask sensitive information such as credit card numbers and national ID numbers before analysts use the data. Which product fits?
Sensitive Data Protection discovers, classifies, and de-identifies sensitive data such as card and ID numbers.

5. Trust and Security with Google Cloud
5.2 Describe the business value of Google's multilayered approach to cloud security
A public website is targeted by DDoS attacks and web exploits such as SQL injection. The company wants protection at Google's network edge. Which product fits?
Cloud Armor provides DDoS protection and web application firewall capabilities at Google's edge.

5. Trust and Security with Google Cloud
5.2 Describe the business value of Google's multilayered approach to cloud security
A company needs a secure, private, high-bandwidth connection between its data center and Google Cloud, rather than sending traffic over the public internet. Which product fits?
Cloud Interconnect provides private, high-bandwidth connectivity between on-premises networks and Google Cloud, while Cloud VPN offers encrypted connections over the internet.

5. Trust and Security with Google Cloud
5.2 Describe the business value of Google's multilayered approach to cloud security
A European company must ensure its data stays in the EU and wants evidence that Google Cloud meets regulatory standards. How does Google Cloud help earn and maintain this trust?
Through data residency controls, digital sovereignty options, third-party audits and certifications, compliance reports, and transparency reports.
By letting customers inspect data centers whenever they like.
By storing data only in one global location.
By keeping all audit results secret.
Google Cloud supports data residency and sovereignty and provides independent audit reports, certifications, and transparency reports.
Secret audits, single-location storage, and unrestricted physical inspections aren't how trust is established.
5. Trust and Security with Google Cloud
5.2 Describe the business value of Google's multilayered approach to cloud security

A German public agency tells its cloud provider: "Our data must be stored only in Germany, and we must also keep control over who can access it, including holding our own encryption keys, so that it is subject only to German and EU law." The project manager thinks storing data in a German region satisfies everything. What should the agency understand?
Data residency and data sovereignty mean the same thing, so choosing a German region is enough.
Data sovereignty is only about which region data is stored in, while data residency is about encryption.

Data residency covers where data is physically stored and processed; data sovereignty goes further, covering who controls and can access the data and which jurisdiction's laws apply, so the agency also needs controls such as customer-held keys and sovereign cloud options.
Neither concept applies to public sector organizations.

Data residency is about the geographic location of data, while data sovereignty concerns control, access, and legal jurisdiction over that data, which is why sovereignty requirements often add measures like customer-managed or externally held keys and sovereign cloud offerings.
Choosing a region addresses residency only, and the other options reverse or dismiss the concepts.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs
A company is moving from buying servers every few years to paying monthly for cloud resources. How does this affect its finances?
It shifts spending from OpEx to CapEx.
It requires buying more hardware upfront.
It shifts spending from capital expenditure (CapEx) to operating expenditure (OpEx), which can lower total cost of ownership by avoiding upfront purchases and idle capacity.
Cloud consumption turns large upfront purchases (CapEx) into ongoing, usage-based costs (OpEx), which can reduce TCO when capacity is used efficiently.
It doesn't eliminate IT costs or require more upfront hardware.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs
A company's cloud bill grew unexpectedly because no one was clearly responsible for monitoring spending. What does Google recommend as a first step in cloud financial governance?
Clearly identify who manages cloud costs, often through a cross-functional team of finance, technology, and business stakeholders, and give them cost management tools.
Let each developer spend without limits.
Review costs only once a year.
Effective cloud financial governance starts with clear ownership and collaboration across finance, technology, and business teams, supported by cost tools.
Abandoning the cloud, unlimited spending, or annual reviews don't control costs.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs
A company has the right cost tools, but costs still rise because teams leave test resources running and nobody reviews spending regularly. What does this illustrate about controlling cloud costs?
Technology alone is enough to control costs.
Cost control requires the combination of people, processes, and technology.
Only the cloud provider can control costs.
Costs can't be controlled in the cloud.
Tools need accountable people and regular processes, such as reviews and cleanup, to be effective.
Costs can be controlled, and customers share that responsibility with the provider's tools.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs
A company wants to organize its Google Cloud resources by department, apply access policies once and have them inherited, and see costs by department. Which feature supports this?
The resource hierarchy of organization, folders, projects, and resources.
The resource hierarchy lets organizations group projects into folders, apply policies that are inherited downward, and gain visibility and control by area.
The other products don't organize resources.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs
A finance team wants to be alerted when a project's monthly spending reaches 50%, 90%, and 100% of a planned amount. Which feature fits?
Cloud Billing budgets with threshold alerts.
Billing budgets send alerts when spending reaches set thresholds of a planned amount.
The other products don't track spending.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs
A company wants to prevent a development project from accidentally creating hundreds of expensive virtual machines. Which control limits how many resources the project can consume?
Quotas cap the amount of specific resources a project can use, preventing runaway consumption.
Budgets alert on spending but don't cap resources, and the other products are unrelated.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs

An AI team needs GPUs for a training job that can start whenever capacity is available, and wants to obtain accelerators efficiently rather than holding expensive capacity idle. Which Google Cloud capability helps?
Dynamic Workload Scheduler helps teams obtain GPUs and TPUs for jobs when capacity is available, improving access and controlling cost.
The other products don't schedule accelerator capacity.
6.2 Describe fundamental concepts of modern operations, reliability, and resilience

Customers report that a web application is slow, but the operations team has no visibility into what's happening. The team wants to collect metrics, set up alerts, and view logs in one place. Which Google Cloud capabilities help?
Google Cloud Observability, including Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging.
Google Cloud Observability provides monitoring, alerting, and logging, plus tools like Cloud Trace and Cloud Profiler for deeper analysis.
The other products don't provide operational visibility.
6.2 Describe fundamental concepts of modern operations, reliability, and resilience

A company promises customers 99.9% availability in its contract, tracks the percentage of successful requests, and sets an internal target of 99.95%. Which terms describe the contract promise, the measurement, and the internal target?
A service level agreement (SLA) is the contractual promise, a service level indicator (SLI) is the metric measured, and a service level objective (SLO) is the internal target.
6.2 Describe fundamental concepts of modern operations, reliability, and resilience
An operations team wants to measure the health of a user-facing service. Which four signals are commonly used to measure performance and reliability?
Storage class, region, zone, and folder.
Revenue, headcount, office space, and travel.
The four golden signals of latency, traffic, errors, and saturation summarize how a service is performing.
The other options aren't reliability metrics.
6.2 Describe fundamental concepts of modern operations, reliability, and resilience
A company wants its order system to keep running if a server or zone fails, and to recover data if it's accidentally deleted. Which practices support resilient infrastructure?
Storing backups on the same server as the data.
Redundancy, replication across zones or regions, scalable infrastructure, and regular backups.
Running everything on a single server.
Redundancy and replication remove single points of failure, scalability handles load, and backups enable recovery from deletion.
6.2 Describe fundamental concepts of modern operations, reliability, and resilience

A company wants development and operations teams to work together more closely, release changes more frequently and reliably, and use engineering practices to manage reliability. Which approaches describe this?
Separating teams so they never communicate.
DevOps emphasizes collaboration and frequent, reliable delivery, and SRE applies engineering practices such as SLOs and error budgets to reliability.
The other options slow delivery or reduce reliability.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs

A company runs a production database server on Compute Engine 24 hours a day and is confident it will keep running at the same size for the next three years. Finance wants the largest discount available in exchange for a commitment. Which option fits?
Committed use discounts (CUDs) with a three-year term.
Committed use discounts give deep savings in exchange for committing to a level of usage for one or three years, which suits steady, predictable workloads.
Sustained use discounts apply automatically but are smaller, Spot VMs can be reclaimed and don't suit a production database, and on-demand pricing has no discount.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs

A company has three workloads: a steady production application that runs all year, a nightly data-processing job that can be interrupted and restarted, and several test VMs that run for most of each month but whose future is uncertain. Which pricing approach best matches each workload?

Committed use discounts for the steady application, Spot VMs for the interruptible nightly job, and on-demand VMs for the test machines, which automatically receive sustained use discounts when they run for a large part of the month (on eligible machine types).
Spot VMs for all three workloads.
Committed use discounts for all three workloads.
On-demand pricing for the steady application, committed use discounts for the nightly job, and Spot VMs for the test machines.

Commitments fit predictable long-term use, Spot VMs fit fault-tolerant work that can be interrupted, and sustained use discounts reward eligible VMs that run for much of the month without any commitment.
Spot for everything risks interrupting production, committing to uncertain test VMs can waste money, and option D reverses the fits.
6.1 Recognize how Google Cloud supports controlling cloud costs

A finance team set a Cloud Billing budget of $10,000 for a development project with an alert at 100%. Spending reached $14,000 anyway, because a script created far more virtual machines than intended. The team assumed the budget would stop the spending. What should they understand?
Budgets automatically shut down all resources at 100%.
Budgets send alerts when spending reaches thresholds but don't cap spending; quotas limit how many resources a project can use, so a quota would have prevented the runaway VM creation.
Quotas send cost alerts, while budgets limit the number of VMs.
Neither budgets nor quotas can help control cloud usage.
Budgets track spending and notify people (and can trigger automation), but on their own they don't stop resources, while quotas put a hard ceiling on resource consumption.
Budgets don't shut resources down automatically, option C reverses the roles, and both tools do help control usage.
1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls

A warehouse posts large signs at every entrance stating that the premises are under 24-hour video surveillance. The cameras record to a server, but no one watches the feeds live. What is the primary control type of the signs?
The signs are meant to discourage someone from attempting an intrusion in the first place, which makes them a deterrent control.
The recorded footage could serve a detective purpose after the fact, but the signs themselves detect nothing, correct nothing, and don't stand in for a missing control.
1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls

A hospital runs a legacy imaging system that can't support multifactor authentication. Until the system is replaced next year, the security team places it on an isolated VLAN with strict access control lists and adds detailed logging of every connection. How should these measures be classified?
Preventive controls that fully satisfy the MFA requirement
Compensating controls are alternative measures used when the required control can't be implemented, reducing risk to an acceptable level in the meantime.
Isolation and extra logging don't fully replace MFA, they aren't policies telling people what to do, and their main purpose isn't discouragement.
1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls
Which of the following is an example of a managerial control?
A security guard at the front desk
Managerial (administrative) controls focus on oversight, planning, and risk management, such as risk assessments and security policies.
Firewalls and antivirus are technical controls, and a guard is a physical or operational control carried out by a person.
1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls
After a ransomware attack encrypts several file servers, the administrators wipe the affected systems and restore them from last night's offline backups. What type of control is the restoration?
Corrective controls restore systems to normal operation after an incident has occurred, which is exactly what restoring from backups does.
Detective controls identify incidents, deterrents discourage them, and preventive controls stop them from happening.
1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls
A company's acceptable use policy states that employees must lock their workstations whenever they step away from their desks. What control type does this policy statement represent?
Directive controls tell people what they must or must not do, typically through policies, procedures, and standards.
The policy doesn't technically enforce the lock (an automatic screen-lock setting would), it doesn't detect anything, and it isn't standing in for a missing control.
1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls
A security manager is classifying the organization's controls by category. Which pair consists of two operational controls?
Security awareness training delivered by the HR team and configuration management procedures followed by system administrators
A web application firewall and an intrusion detection system
The information security policy and the annual risk assessment
Operational controls are implemented and carried out primarily by people, such as running awareness training or following configuration management procedures.
Firewalls, IDS, encryption, and MFA are technical controls, while policies and risk assessments are managerial controls.
An attacker intercepts a payment file sent between two banks and changes the destination account number before it arrives. Which element of the CIA triad was violated?
Integrity ensures data isn't altered in an unauthorized way, and changing the account number is unauthorized modification.
Confidentiality concerns disclosure, availability concerns access to the data or service, and non-repudiation isn't part of the CIA triad.

A finance department needs to be able to prove that a specific manager approved each wire transfer, so that the manager can't later claim the approval came from someone else. Which concept and mechanism meet this need?
Confidentiality, through encrypting the approval message
Non-repudiation, through digital signatures using the manager's private key
Non-repudiation provides proof of origin, and a digital signature created with a private key only that manager holds ties the approval to them.
Encryption protects secrecy, redundancy protects uptime, and RBAC controls who may approve but doesn't prove who actually did.

A company is implementing a zero trust architecture. When a user requests access to a finance application, one component evaluates the request against policy, using the user's identity, device health, and threat intelligence, and decides whether to allow it. Which component makes this decision?
In the zero trust control plane, the policy engine evaluates requests against policy and decides whether to grant access, and the policy administrator then communicates that decision.

The policy enforcement point sits in the data plane and carries out the decision, the implicit trust zone is the area behind the enforcement point, and the subject is the user or system making the request.

A security analyst places a file named "2026_Executive_Salaries.xlsx" on a file share. No legitimate user has any reason to open it, and any access to it triggers an alert. What is this deception technique called?
A honeyfile is a decoy file designed to attract attackers and alert defenders when someone accesses it.
A honeypot is a decoy system, a honeynet is a network of decoy systems, and a honeytoken is fake data, such as a credential or record, planted to detect its use.

A new CISO compares the organization's existing security controls against the target profile it wants to achieve under the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, listing the controls that are missing or immature. What is this activity?
A gap analysis compares the current state against a desired state or framework to identify what's missing.
Penetration tests and vulnerability scans look for exploitable technical weaknesses, and risk transfer shifts risk to another party, such as an insurer.

A user signs in to a VPN with a password and a hardware token, is granted access only to the engineering file servers, and the VPN concentrator logs how long the session lasted and how much data was transferred. Which part of AAA does the logging represent?
Accounting tracks what a user did, such as session duration and data transferred, for auditing.

Authentication verified the user with the password and token, authorization limited access to the engineering servers, and identification is the claim of identity (the username) that precedes authentication.
1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes

An approved firmware upgrade to the core switches fails halfway through the maintenance window, leaving the network unstable. The team has no documented steps for returning the switches to their previous state, so the outage runs into business hours. Which element of change management was missing?
A backout plan documents how to reverse a change and restore the previous state if the change fails.
Impact analysis predicts effects before the change, a stakeholder list identifies who is affected, and an SOP covers routine repeatable tasks rather than recovery from this specific change.
1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes

Before the change advisory board approves a patch to the payroll database, the requester documents which applications and users will be affected, the risks of applying the patch, and the risks of not applying it. What is this step?
Impact analysis evaluates how a change affects systems, users, and risk, including the risk of not making the change, so approvers can make an informed decision.
A backout plan covers reversal, version control tracks changes to files, and a maintenance window is when the change is scheduled.
1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes

A security patch for the customer portal requires restarting the web service. The operations team agrees with business owners to apply it every second Sunday between 2:00 and 4:00 a.m., when traffic is lowest. What change management concept does this describe?
A maintenance window is a pre-agreed time for making changes that minimizes impact on users.
Ownership identifies who is responsible for the change, an allow list controls what can run, and test results show whether the change worked in testing.
1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes

During review of a proposed TLS library upgrade on an API server, an engineer discovers that a billing service and a reporting job both load the same library and haven't been tested with the new version. Which technical implication of change management does this finding relate to most directly?
Dependencies are other systems or components that rely on the item being changed and may break as a result, so they must be identified and tested.
Restricted activities limit what can be done during a change, downtime concerns service interruption, and an allow list controls which software may run.
1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes

After an outage, auditors ask who changed a firewall configuration file, what exactly was changed, and when. The team needs a way to answer this quickly in the future and to roll back to any earlier configuration. What should the team implement?
Version control records every change with author, time, and content, and allows reverting to earlier versions.
Allow listing controls executable software, a change owner is accountable for a change but doesn't record history, and an SOP describes how to perform a task.
1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions

A company is building an internal certificate authority. It needs to generate and store the CA's private signing key in dedicated, tamper-resistant hardware that performs cryptographic operations without ever exposing the key, and that can serve many applications. What should it use?
A software key store on the CA server
An HSM is a dedicated, tamper-resistant device or appliance designed to generate, store, and use keys for high-value services like certificate authorities.
A TPM is a chip tied to a single device, a secure enclave is a protected area within a processor, and a software key store doesn't offer hardware protection.
1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions

An attacker steals a database of password hashes and uses precomputed rainbow tables to crack many of them quickly, because several users share the same password and therefore the same hash. What should the developers add so that identical passwords produce different hashes and rainbow tables become ineffective?
A salt is a unique random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables don't match.

Key stretching slows down each guess and is a useful addition, but it doesn't by itself make identical passwords hash differently. Tokenization replaces data with tokens, and steganography hides data inside other files.
1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions

A web browser must check whether a server's certificate has been revoked. To avoid downloading a large list of revoked certificates, it sends a query about that single certificate and receives a signed "good", "revoked", or "unknown" response. Which mechanism is the browser using?
OCSP returns the real-time status of a single certificate, avoiding the download of a full revocation list.
A CRL is the full list of revoked certificates published by the CA, a CSR is a request to obtain a certificate, and a wildcard certificate covers multiple subdomains.
1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions

Two branch offices need to agree on a shared symmetric session key over the internet. They have no pre-shared secret, and anyone could be watching the traffic. Which technique lets them derive the same key without ever sending it across the network?
Hashing the key with SHA-256 before sending it
Diffie-Hellman key exchange, such as ECDHE
Diffie-Hellman lets two parties each compute the same secret from exchanged public values, so the key itself never crosses the network; the ephemeral variant also provides forward secrecy.
A hash can't be turned back into a usable key, steganography only hides data, and salting is used for password storage.
1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions

An online retailer wants to reduce its PCI DSS scope. It replaces stored card numbers in its order database with random values that have no mathematical relationship to the originals. The real numbers are kept only in a separate, highly protected vault that maps each value back to its card. Which technique is this?
Tokenization substitutes sensitive data with tokens that can only be mapped back through a secure vault, removing real card data from most systems.
Hashing is one-way with no lookup back to the original, masking hides part of the value on display, and encrypted data is mathematically derived from the original and still in scope.
1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions
A company needs one TLS certificate that will work for www.example.com, shop.example.com, mail.example.com, and any subdomains it adds later. Which type of certificate fits best?
A wildcard certificate secures every first-level subdomain of a domain, including ones added later.
A self-signed certificate won't be trusted by public browsers, a code-signing certificate signs software rather than securing websites, and a root CA certificate is used to issue other certificates.
1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions
Which statement correctly describes asymmetric encryption used to send a confidential message?
The sender encrypts with their own private key, and anyone can decrypt with the sender's public key.
Both parties use the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt.
The sender encrypts with the recipient's public key, and only the recipient's private key can decrypt it.
The message is hashed, so it can't be read by anyone.
For confidentiality, data is encrypted with the recipient's public key so that only the holder of the matching private key can decrypt it.
Encrypting with your own private key creates a digital signature, which proves origin but not secrecy. A shared key is symmetric encryption, and hashing is one-way, not encryption.
2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

A defense contractor finds that an attacker has quietly been inside its network for 14 months. The attacker used a custom zero-day exploit and exfiltrated engineering designs in small amounts to avoid detection. Which threat actor is most likely responsible?
Long-term stealth, custom zero-days, and theft of defense designs point to a well-funded nation-state actor (an advanced persistent threat) motivated by espionage.
Hacktivists seek publicity, unskilled attackers use existing tools noisily, and nothing suggests the attacker started with internal access.
2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations
A chemical company's website is defaced with a message condemning its environmental record, and the group responsible posts a manifesto on social media. Which threat actor fits best?
Hacktivists attack to promote a political or philosophical cause and usually seek publicity.
Organized crime is driven by money, shadow IT is unauthorized technology use by employees, and nation-states typically avoid public attribution.
2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

To work faster, a marketing team signs up for an unapproved file-sharing service with a company credit card and uploads customer contact lists to it. IT and security are unaware of the service. What is this an example of?
An insider threat motivated by revenge
Shadow IT is the use of technology without the knowledge or approval of IT, which creates unmanaged risk even when the intent is harmless.
There's no malicious motive here, so revenge, hacktivism, and organized crime don't fit.
2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

A ransomware group encrypts a hospital's systems, demands payment in cryptocurrency, and offers a "customer support" chat to help victims pay. It runs affiliate programs much like a business. What is this group's primary motivation?
Organized criminal groups running ransomware operate like businesses, and their goal is money.
There's no political message, no intelligence collection, and no personal grievance against the victim.
2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

The IDS records a flood of noisy, well-known exploit attempts against a web server, copied from a public exploit site and aimed at software the server doesn't even run. Which threat actor is most likely?
Unskilled attackers rely on existing tools and scripts without understanding them, so their attempts are noisy and poorly targeted.
Nation-states and organized crime groups tend to be stealthy and targeted, and nothing indicates internal access.
2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations
A database administrator learns he'll be laid off next month. He schedules a script that will delete production tables 30 days after his account is disabled. Which description best fits this threat?
An unskilled attacker using public tools
An insider threat with internal access and a revenge motive
The administrator is an insider who uses legitimate access and knowledge of internal systems, motivated by revenge; the delayed script is a logic bomb.
The other actors are external and don't match the personal grievance.
2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations
Which attribute best explains why insider threats are often harder to detect than external attackers?
Insiders already have legitimate access and knowledge of internal systems and processes.
Insiders always have more funding than external groups.
Insiders are usually backed by nation-states.
Insiders rely mainly on zero-day exploits.
Because insiders use legitimate credentials and know where valuable data lives, their activity can look like normal work.
Funding, nation-state backing, and zero-day use aren't typical characteristics of insiders.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces
Employees receive text messages claiming a package couldn't be delivered, with a link to "reschedule delivery" that leads to a page requesting their corporate login. What type of attack is this?
Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS text message.
Vishing uses voice calls, whaling targets senior executives, and typosquatting relies on look-alike domain names that users type by mistake.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces
An attacker registers "micr0soft-support.com" and "rnicrosoft.com", hoping users who mistype or misread the real domain will land on credential-harvesting pages. What is this technique?
Typosquatting registers domains that resemble legitimate ones to catch typing or reading mistakes.
A watering hole compromises a site victims already visit, BEC uses compromised or spoofed business email to commit fraud, and pretexting is an invented scenario used to manipulate someone.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

Attackers want into a regional power utility but can't get past its email filtering. They compromise an industry association website that the utility's engineers visit regularly and plant malicious code that infects visitors from the utility's IP range. What type of attack is this?
A watering hole attack compromises a website the target group already trusts and visits, then infects those visitors.
No message was sent to the victims, and no one was impersonated or given a false story.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

A caller claims to be from the IT help desk and explains that the company is "migrating mailboxes tonight." He asks the employee to read back the MFA code that's about to arrive so the account won't be locked. Which social engineering technique is he relying on most?
Pretexting creates a believable invented scenario (here a mailbox migration) to persuade the victim to hand over information.
It's delivered by phone, which also makes it vishing, but it isn't a compromised website, a look-alike domain, or a text message.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

During a security assessment, testers leave USB drives labeled "Q3 Layoffs – Confidential" in the company parking lot. Several employees plug them into their workstations. Which threat vector is being tested?
Dropping infected USB drives exploits removable devices as a threat vector and relies on curiosity (baiting).
It isn't delivered over a network or through messages, and it doesn't involve a vendor or supplier.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

Attackers breach a network management software vendor's build system and insert a backdoor into a legitimate, digitally signed update. Thousands of customers install the update automatically. What best describes this attack vector?
Vulnerable software on the client systems
A supply chain attack through a software provider
Compromising a vendor so that malicious code reaches customers through trusted updates is a supply chain attack via a software provider.
The customers' software wasn't inherently flawed, and no open ports or default credentials were exploited.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

In a hotel lobby near a corporate office, an attacker sets up a wireless access point broadcasting the company's guest network SSID with a stronger signal, then captures the traffic of employees who connect. What is this?
An evil twin is a rogue access point impersonating a legitimate SSID to trick devices into connecting, which exploits unsecure wireless networks.
It doesn't use Bluetooth or wired connections, and no trusted website was compromised.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

An internet-wide scan finds hundreds of a company's IP cameras exposing their web interface, many still accepting the manufacturer's username "admin" and password "admin". Which attack surface does this describe most precisely?
The decisive weakness is the unchanged manufacturer credentials, which let anyone log in.
Open ports make the interface reachable but aren't the core problem, nothing says the cameras are unsupported, and image-based vectors hide malicious code in image files.
2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

An accounts payable clerk receives an email from a real supplier's mailbox, which attackers had compromised. It says the supplier's bank details have changed and asks for this month's invoice to be paid to a new account. Which attack is this?
Business email compromise uses compromised or spoofed business email accounts to trick staff into fraudulent payments or data disclosure.
It's email rather than SMS, no website was compromised, and the attacker used the real supplier's mailbox rather than impersonating a brand.

A privileged backup utility checks that a user has permission to read a file and then, a few milliseconds later, opens the file. An attacker repeatedly swaps the file for a symbolic link to /etc/shadow during that gap and eventually reads the protected file. Which vulnerability is being exploited?
A TOC/TOU race condition happens when the state of a resource changes between the moment it's checked and the moment it's used.
Nothing overflows a buffer, no database query is manipulated, and no code is injected into another process's memory.
A tester enters `' OR '1'='1' --` into the username field of a login page and is logged in as the first user in the database without a valid password. Which vulnerability does this demonstrate?
The input changes the logic of the database query because the application builds SQL from unsanitized input; parameterized queries prevent this.
XSS runs script in other users' browsers, directory traversal reaches files outside the web root, and a buffer overflow writes past allocated memory.

An attacker posts a comment on a support forum that contains hidden JavaScript. Every user who views the thread has the script run in their browser, which sends their session cookie to the attacker's server. What vulnerability does the forum have?
Stored XSS saves malicious script on the site and runs it in the browser of everyone who views the page; output encoding and input validation prevent it.
SQL injection targets the database, CSRF tricks a user's browser into sending an unwanted request, and a race condition depends on timing.

A cloud provider patches a hypervisor flaw that let code running inside one customer's guest virtual machine execute commands on the underlying host, putting every other tenant's VMs on that host at risk. What type of vulnerability was this?
VM escape breaks out of a guest VM's isolation to reach the hypervisor or host.
Resource reuse leaves data in memory or storage that's reassigned to another tenant, while side loading and jailbreaking are mobile device issues.

A researcher discovers that a company's cloud storage bucket of database backups can be listed and downloaded by anyone on the internet. The storage service itself has no software flaw. What type of vulnerability is this?
Public access to the bucket is a configuration mistake by the customer, not a flaw in the provider's software, and it's one of the most common causes of cloud data exposure.
There's no unknown software bug, weak algorithm, or compromised hardware.
Attackers begin exploiting a flaw in a popular VPN appliance before the vendor knows it exists. No patch or official workaround is available. How is this vulnerability classified?
A zero-day vulnerability is unknown to the vendor, or has no fix available, when it's exploited.
The appliance is current and supported, so it isn't legacy or end-of-life, and the issue is a code flaw rather than a configuration error.

A manufacturer's production line is controlled by PCs running an operating system version the vendor stopped supporting three years ago. New vulnerabilities in that OS are published, but no patches will ever be released for it. What vulnerability does this describe?
End-of-life systems that no longer receive security updates
End-of-life (and legacy) systems stay exposed to every newly found vulnerability because the vendor no longer patches them; compensating controls such as isolation are needed until replacement.
The flaws are publicly known, so this isn't a zero-day, and nothing involves timing or reused resources.

An employee installs a "free premium" version of a paid app on her company-managed Android phone by downloading an APK file from a third-party website instead of the official app store. What is this practice called?
Side loading installs apps from outside the official store, bypassing its security vetting.

Jailbreaking removes the operating system's built-in restrictions (rooting is the Android equivalent), bluesnarfing steals data over Bluetooth, and a malicious update comes through a legitimate update channel.
An audit finds that an internal payments application only supports TLS 1.0 and signs its records with MD5. Both are known to be broken. What category of vulnerability is this?
Cryptographic vulnerability caused by weak or deprecated algorithms
Relying on deprecated protocols and broken hash functions is a cryptographic vulnerability that enables downgrade, interception, and collision attacks.
The problem lies in the algorithms, not the cloud, process memory, or a supplier.

An attacker sends input longer than a program's fixed-size memory area, overwriting adjacent memory, including the function's return address, so that execution jumps to the attacker's code. What is this vulnerability?
A buffer overflow writes data past the end of allocated memory and can redirect execution; bounds checking and memory protections such as ASLR and DEP reduce the risk.
Privilege escalation may be the result of an exploit, but it isn't the vulnerability itself.
A user downloads a "free PDF converter" that works as advertised but also quietly installs a remote access tool, giving the attacker control of the laptop. What type of malware is this?
A trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it.
A worm spreads by itself, a logic bomb waits for a trigger condition, and a rootkit hides its presence with deep system access.

Within an hour, malware spreads from one unpatched server to 400 others across the network by exploiting a remote file-sharing vulnerability, with no user clicking or opening anything. Which type of malware is this?
Worms replicate across networks on their own by exploiting vulnerabilities, without user interaction.
Viruses need a user to run an infected file, trojans rely on being installed, and spyware focuses on collecting information.

Incident responders find a server that is sending data to an unknown host, yet the operating system's process list and file listings show nothing unusual. When they boot the disk from trusted external media, they find modified kernel drivers. Which malware is most likely present?
Rootkits gain deep, often kernel-level, access and hide processes, files, and connections from the running operating system, which is why offline analysis exposed them.
Keyloggers record keystrokes, bloatware is unwanted preinstalled software, and adware shows advertisements.
The identity provider logs a successful sign-in to an employee's account from Chicago at 09:02, followed by another from Singapore at 09:20. Which indicator of malicious activity is this?
Impossible travel flags sign-ins from locations too far apart to reach in the time between them, which suggests stolen credentials.
Lockouts follow repeated failures, resource inaccessibility means systems can't be reached, and out-of-cycle logging is log activity at unusual times.

Over two days, the authentication logs show a single failed login for each of 3,000 different accounts. Every attempt uses the password "Autumn2026!", and the attempts are spread out to stay below the lockout threshold. Which attack is this?
Password spraying tries one or a few common passwords against many accounts, avoiding the lockouts that many guesses against one account would trigger.
Brute force tries many passwords against one account, a birthday attack targets hash collisions, and credential replay reuses captured credentials or tokens.

A company's website is overwhelmed by large DNS responses it never requested. Analysis shows attackers sent small queries to thousands of open DNS resolvers using the company's IP address as the spoofed source. What type of attack is this?

Spoofing the victim's address so third-party servers send it far larger responses is a reflected, amplified DDoS. DNS poisoning corrupts resolver records, an on-path attack intercepts traffic, and a replay attack resends captured data.
The web application firewall logs show requests such as `GET /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd`. What is the attacker attempting?
Directory traversal uses "../" sequences to climb out of the web directory and read files elsewhere on the server.
There's no SQL, no script for a browser to run, and nothing aimed at overflowing memory.

On a public network, an attacker interferes with the TLS handshake so that a client and server that both support TLS 1.3 end up negotiating an older protocol version with weak ciphers, which the attacker can then break. Which attack is this?
A downgrade attack forces systems onto an older, weaker protocol or cipher; disabling legacy protocols on servers prevents it.
Collision and birthday attacks target hash functions, and replay attacks resend captured traffic.

While investigating a suspected intrusion, an analyst notices that the domain controller's security event log has no entries at all between 01:10 and 04:30, although the server was running and normally logs hundreds of events an hour. What indicator is this?
An unexplained gap in logs from a running system often means an attacker cleared or stopped logging to hide activity.
Blocked content means security tools stopped something, resource consumption is unusual CPU, memory, or bandwidth use, and concurrent sessions are the same account active in several places at once.

An attacker captures a user's NTLM password hash from a compromised workstation and uses it to authenticate to a file server, without ever learning the user's actual password. What type of attack is this?
Credential replay reuses captured authentication material, here a password hash, to log in as the victim.
Spraying guesses passwords, a downgrade weakens protocol negotiation, and RFID cloning copies physical access badges.
2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques

A hotel's self-check-in kiosks should run only the check-in application. Security wants to block every other program from executing, including malware nobody has seen before. Which mitigation fits best?
An allow list permits only approved applications to run and blocks everything else, including unknown malware, which suits single-purpose systems.
Signatures and deny lists only stop known-bad software, and an IDS detects activity rather than preventing execution.
2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques

A retailer moves its point-of-sale terminals onto their own VLAN, separated from the guest Wi-Fi and the corporate office network, with a firewall allowing only the traffic the payment processor needs. Which mitigation is this?
Segmentation divides the network into zones with controlled traffic between them, limiting how far an attacker can move and reducing compliance scope.
Nothing is being retired, encrypted, or simply watched.
2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques

The EDR console shows ransomware behavior on a finance laptop. The responder immediately cuts the laptop off from the network but leaves it powered on so memory can be captured for forensics. Which mitigation technique is this?
Isolation separates a compromised system to stop the threat spreading while preserving evidence.
Patching fixes vulnerabilities, decommissioning permanently retires assets, and configuration enforcement keeps systems at an approved baseline.
2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques

An audit finds that help desk technicians are members of the Domain Admins group, even though their only privileged task is resetting user passwords. Security creates a delegated role that allows password resets only. Which principle is being applied?
Least privilege grants only the access needed to perform a job, which reduces the damage from mistakes or compromised accounts.
Job rotation and mandatory vacations help uncover fraud, and implicit trust is the opposite of a least-privilege, zero-trust approach.
2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques
An administrator is preparing a new Linux web server for production. Which set of actions best represents system hardening?
Installing extra monitoring tools, enabling every available service, and keeping the vendor's default passwords for support
Removing unnecessary software, disabling unused ports and services, changing default passwords, and enabling a host-based firewall
Placing the server in the DMZ and leaving its configuration at vendor defaults
Taking a full backup and documenting the server in the asset inventory
Hardening reduces the attack surface by removing what isn't needed, closing unused ports and services, replacing default credentials, and adding host protections.
Enabling everything and keeping defaults does the opposite, and backups and inventory are good practice but don't harden the system.
2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques

A company is retiring storage arrays that held customer records. The drives are cryptographically erased and then physically shredded, the arrays are removed from the asset inventory, and their management certificates are revoked. What process is this?
Decommissioning securely retires assets, including data sanitization, inventory updates, and removal of credentials or certificates, so they can't become a forgotten risk.
The arrays aren't being contained, updated, or placed in a network zone.
2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques

A company wants its laptops to detect suspicious behavior such as process injection and credential dumping. It also wants analysts to be able to isolate a laptop remotely and review a timeline of what happened on it. Which hardening control should it deploy?
EDR monitors endpoint behavior, raises alerts on suspicious activity, supports remote isolation, and records telemetry for investigation.
A host firewall filters network traffic, full-disk encryption protects data at rest, and deny lists block only known software.
2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques

After a hardening project, administrators find that servers gradually drift back to insecure settings as people make manual changes. The company deploys a tool that continuously checks each server against the approved baseline and automatically reverts unauthorized changes. Which mitigation is this?
Configuration enforcement keeps systems at their approved baseline and corrects drift automatically.
Monitoring alone would report the drift without fixing it, least privilege limits access rights, and decommissioning retires systems.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models

A company runs its web application on virtual machines in a public cloud infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) offering. Under the cloud responsibility matrix, who is responsible for patching the operating systems on those VMs?
Nobody, because the cloud patches VMs automatically
In IaaS, the provider secures the physical infrastructure and hypervisor, while the customer manages the guest operating system, applications, data, and access.
The provider doesn't patch customers' guest OS images.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models
An organization moves its email to a software-as-a-service (SaaS) provider. Which security responsibility remains with the organization?
Physical security of the data center
Managing user accounts, access permissions, and how data is shared
In SaaS, the provider runs the infrastructure and application, but the customer still controls identities, access, configuration, and its own data.
Servers, data centers, and hypervisors are the provider's responsibility.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models

A cloud team stops building environments by clicking through the console. Instead, it defines networks, firewall rules, and servers in version-controlled templates that are reviewed and scanned before deployment. What is the main security benefit of this infrastructure-as-code (IaC) approach?
It removes the need for any access controls
It guarantees that no vulnerabilities exist in the code
Environments are consistent, reviewable, and repeatable, which reduces misconfiguration and drift
It makes the infrastructure physically isolated
IaC makes configuration consistent, auditable, and testable before deployment, reducing human error and drift.
It still needs access controls, its templates can contain flaws (which is why they're scanned), and it doesn't provide physical isolation.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models
A team moves its image-processing job to serverless functions. Which security responsibility does the team still own?
Patching the underlying server operating system
Securing the function code, its dependencies, and the permissions granted to the function
Capacity planning for the servers that run the functions

With serverless, the provider manages servers, operating systems, and scaling, but the customer remains responsible for application code, third-party libraries, and the identity and permissions each function uses.
The other options belong to the provider.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models
A company breaks a monolithic application into 40 microservices that call each other over APIs. Which security implication should the architects plan for?
The attack surface shrinks because only one service is exposed
Service-to-service communication no longer needs authentication
Patching becomes unnecessary because services are small
More APIs and network connections increase the attack surface, so each service needs authentication, authorization, and encrypted communication

Microservices add many internal APIs, each a potential entry point, so they need service identities, least-privilege permissions, and encryption such as mutual TLS. The benefit is a smaller blast radius per service, but only if those controls are in place.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models

A nuclear plant's safety control system must have no network connection at all to the corporate network or the internet. Software updates are carried in on controlled, scanned media. What architecture is this?
An air gap physically isolates a system from other networks.
VLANs and SDN provide logical separation over shared hardware, and hybrid cloud connects on-premises systems to the cloud.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models

A data center adopts software-defined networking (SDN). A central controller programs forwarding behavior on all switches and applies segmentation policies. From a security perspective, which component becomes the highest-value target?
The SDN controller, which runs the control plane
The data-plane forwarding tables on a single switch
SDN centralizes control, so compromising the controller can change traffic and security policy across the entire network.
It needs strong access control, hardening, and redundancy. Individual ports or switches affect much less.
